title: Sadhu Sundar Singh
hookLine: a Sikh-born Indian who became a wandering Christian holy man in saffron robes

lines: A MAN FAINTS ON A PLATFORM.
THE SAME WATER, HIS OWN VESSEL.
cards: A traveler on a hot day in India collapses on a railway platform. Someone runs for water and comes back with it in a cup that belongs to the railway. The man on the ground, half fainting, refuses to drink.
Not because he isn't thirsty. Because of the cup. Then someone brings the same water in his own brass vessel, and he drinks it gladly.
A wandering holy man in a saffron robe told that story, to say something about the gospel and India.

teach.h: A SIKH BOYHOOD, A MOTHER'S DEATH.
teach.b: Sundar Singh grew up in a Sikh family in the Punjab. His mother, by his own telling, took him to hear holy men and read sacred writings, and he loved her deeply.
When she died he was young, and in his grief he grew angry at everything, including the Christian missionaries' book, which by his own account he tore and burned.

teach.h: A NIGHT OF PRAYER, A VISION.
teach.b: Then, his story goes, he prayed through a night asking God to show himself, and before dawn he saw Jesus. He became a Christian. His family could not accept it, and he left home.

teach.h: THE SAFFRON ROBE OF A SADHU.
teach.b: India already had a figure everyone recognized: the sadhu, the wandering holy man with no possessions, walking village to village in a saffron robe. Sundar Singh put on that robe.
He walked barefoot, slept where he was offered a place, and told stories about Jesus in the languages of the villages.
He went over the mountain passes into Tibet to preach, and from his last journey there he never came back. Nobody knows what happened to him.
The railway story answered a question: why does the gospel sometimes sound foreign in India? Because, he said, it had been handed over in a European cup. The water was what people needed.
Jesus told a woman at a well, in the King James Bible: "But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst."

teach.h: THE WATER IN AN INDIAN CUP.
teach.b: That water, Sundar Singh said, can come in an Indian cup. Christians still disagree about how much of a culture the gospel should wear. His answer was a saffron robe and bare feet.

how: Christians in South Asia worship in many styles, and some use Indian forms such as sitting on the floor, bhajan-style songs and saffron dress for those who live as wandering preachers.

games.why: in Sundar Singh's story the man drank gladly from his own vessel. the water, he said, can come in an Indian cup.

practice: Ask yourself what shape stillness takes in your life: a song from your grandmother's kitchen, a language you speak only at home, sitting cross-legged, kneeling or walking. For these two minutes, use your own cup.
If you pray, pray in the words and posture that feel like home; if you don't, sit the way your body knows best.
